column2: The range of sample sizes compatible with this procedure at the target voxel size and geometric configuration. The upper bound is a hard constraint set by the instrument field of view (FOV) at the procedure's target magnification: FOV ≈ detector array width × pixel size / geometric magnification (divide additionally by optical objective multiplier for Versa-class systems using optical magnification). For Mode A (single-volume): all three sample dimensions must fall within the FOV. For Mode B (multi-volume stitching): sample diameter must fall within the FOV; sample length along the rotation axis is effectively unlimited through stitching. The lower bound is a practical guideline: ~10 voxels across the smallest dimension.
column6: e.g., 'Single-volume: max 20 mm in all dimensions at 7.6 µm voxel' | 'Multi-volume stitching: max 25 mm diameter, unlimited length at 12.9 µm voxel' | 'Max 5 mm (all axes) at 0.85 µm voxel with 4× objective'

column2: X-ray tube accelerating voltage in kilovolts (kV). If the voltage was varied across samples within the same procedure or session, report the full range applied (e.g., 90–115 kV). Note: some sources report this parameter as 'X keV' (maximum Bremsstrahlung photon energy) rather than 'X kV' (tube voltage). For polychromatic lab XCT, these are numerically equivalent: E_max [keV] = V [kV]. Record the value as originally reported, and add a parenthetical note if the unit used is keV.
column6: e.g., 80 kV | 130 kV | 160 kV | 190 kV; for variable settings: 90–115 kV
column10: Determines the maximum X-ray photon energy and controls penetration depth and phase contrast. Higher voltages provide greater penetration for dense or large samples; lower voltages improve contrast between low-density phases.
column20: 120 keV (reported in paper as 'accelerating voltage of 120 keV'; likely typo for 120 kV)
column21: 160 keV (paper reports as X-ray photon energy; equivalent to 160 kV tube voltage)

column2: X-ray tube current in microamperes (µA). If the current was varied across samples within the same procedure or session, report the full range applied (e.g., 65–115 µA).
column6: e.g., 89 µA | 108 µA | 180 µA; for variable settings: 65–115 µA
column10: Controls photon flux and therefore projection image SNR. Higher current improves SNR but increases thermal loading on the source and may increase focal spot size.
column18: 179 mA (possibly typo for µA per source)

column2: X-ray tube power in watts (W). Derivable as voltage (kV) × current (mA) = kV × µA / 1000. If power was varied across samples within the session, report the full range applied (e.g., 7–13 W).
column6: e.g., 9 W | 14 W | 25 W; for variable settings: 7–13 W
column10: Power constrains the achievable focal spot size for microfocal tubes: higher power requires a larger focal spot, trading spatial resolution for SNR. Retained as a standalone field because it is routinely reported in the literature and directly constrains instrument operating limits.

column2: Material and thickness of the beam-hardening filter placed between the X-ray source and the sample. Both filter material and thickness must be reported. Instrument-proprietary filter codes should be decoded where possible.
column6: e.g., '1 mm Cu' | '0.72 mm Al' | '2 mm Al' | 'LE2 (calcium fluoride, CaF₂, Zeiss)' | 'HE1 (copper composite, Zeiss)' | 'None'
column10: Hardens the beam by attenuating low-energy photons, reducing beam hardening artifacts and improving CT number stability across the sample.
column17: None (steel sleeve acts as effective filter)
column19: 0.1–0.25 mm Al (Bennu PE protocol range stated)

column2: Distance from the X-ray source focal spot to the centre of the sample rotation axis, in mm.
column6: e.g., 12 mm | 55 mm | 83 mm | 150 mm
column10: Together with SDD, determines geometric magnification (M = SDD/SOD). Shorter SOD increases magnification and reduces voxel size.
column23: N (optimized for 2.06 µm/px; exact value not stated)

column2: Distance from the X-ray source focal spot to the detector surface, in mm. Voxel size ≈ detector pixel size / M (before binning; divide additionally by optical objective for Versa-class systems).
column10: Together with SOD, determines geometric magnification M = SDD/SOD.

column2: Isotropic voxel edge length of the reconstructed 3D volume in micrometres. The target voxel size is set based on the smallest feature to be resolved (target voxel size ≤ ~1/3 of that feature size; see the criterion recorded under Partial Volume Effect Criteria). Record the achieved voxel size as reported by the reconstruction software, which may differ slightly from the target due to final geometric calibration.
column6: e.g., 0.85 µm | 7.63 µm | 22.44 µm (isotropic); "µm/pixel" is an acceptable equivalent for isotropic scans; for anisotropic voxels: "5 µm × 5 µm × 8 µm"; µm³ and µm³/voxel denote voxel volume — do not use for voxel size
column16: N (voxel size not stated; see Ketcham et al. 2022)
column17: N (voxel size not stated; same as 73002 per paper; see Ketcham et al. 2022)

column2: Total angular range over which projection images are acquired, in degrees.
column10: Full 360° rotation is standard for cone-beam lab XCT. 180° rotation (half-scan) is sometimes used for faster acquisition but may introduce additional artifacts.

column2: Total number of equally-spaced projection images acquired over the full rotation range. For Mode B (multi-volume stitching), this is the number per sub-volume.
column10: More projections improve reconstruction quality by reducing under-sampling streak artifacts but increase scan time.
column22: N (0.4° step, 360° implied = 900 views; not stated directly)

column2: Angular increment between successive projection images, in degrees. Equal to Rotation Range divided by Number of Projections when both are reported; however, some sources report step size as the primary rotation parameter without stating the total number of projections explicitly.
column10: Finer step sizes improve angular sampling and reduce streak artifacts at the cost of longer scan time.

column2: Duration of X-ray exposure for each individual projection image frame, in seconds. Adjustment is warranted for samples that are unusually dense or unusually transparent. If the exposure time was varied across samples within the same procedure or session, report the full range applied (e.g., 0.5–2 s).
column6: e.g., 0.5 s | 1.42 s | 6 s | 28 s; for variable settings: 0.5–2 s
column10: Set as a deliberate choice for the target sample type and voxel size: longer exposures increase SNR at the cost of total scan time.

column2: Number of individual detector frames acquired and averaged to produce each saved projection image. The effective exposure per projection = exposure time per frame × frames averaged.
column10: Frame averaging reduces random electronic noise.
column23: ~200 reference (blank) images taken; number of frames averaged per projection N

column2: Detector pixel binning factor applied during acquisition. Binning combines adjacent pixels (e.g., 2×2 combines 4 pixels into one).
column6: 1×1 (no binning) | 2×2 | 4×4 | N/A | None
column10: Reduces effective resolution while increasing per-pixel SNR and reducing file size.

column2: Whether dark-field (detector read with X-ray source off; electronic noise baseline) and bright-field (source on, no sample; gain calibration) reference images are acquired and applied to normalize detector response before reconstruction.
column6: e.g., 'Yes — flat-field applied; residual Poisson noise from flat-fielding noted' | 'No — flux normalization not applied' | N/A | None
column10: Standard practice in all quantitative lab XCT.

column2: Whether projection images are acquired during continuous sample rotation (faster; may introduce slight motion blur at high rotation speeds) or at discrete step positions with the stage stationary during each exposure (stop-and-shoot; eliminates motion blur).
column6: Step rotation (stop-and-shoot) | Continuous rotation | N/A | None
column10: Continuous rotation has been associated with sub-volume rotational mismatch artifacts in multi-volume stitching workflows (Eckley et al. 2025).
column17: Non-continuous rotation (to avoid rotational mismatch of continuous mode)

column2: Total number of overlapping sub-volume scans acquired to cover the full sample length. Applies only to Mode B (multi-volume stitching).
column10: The number of sub-volumes depends on the length of the specific sample being scanned and cannot be fixed in the procedure in advance.

column2: Minimum number of reconstructed slices that must overlap between adjacent sub-volumes in a stitched dataset.
column10: Eckley et al. (2025) report that 500 slices of overlap were used in the Apollo 73001 stitching workflow, while 180 slices proved insufficient for their cone-beam geometry.

column2: Total elapsed time for the complete XCT acquisition, from the start of the first projection to the end of the last. For multi-volume acquisitions, this is the combined scan time across all sub-volumes (not including setup or reconstruction time).
column6: e.g., 37 min | 1.5 h | 240 min
column10: Useful for assessing beam stability and sample integrity concerns over long scans.

column2: Mathematical algorithm used to reconstruct the 3D CT volume from 2D projection images.
column6: FDK (Feldkamp-Davis-Kress, cone-beam) | FBP (filtered back-projection, parallel-beam) | Iterative reconstruction | SART | N/A | None
column10: The Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm is standard for cone-beam lab XCT geometry; iterative methods offer better artifact suppression at the cost of computation time.

column2: Convolution (apodization) filter kernel applied during back-projection reconstruction.
column6: e.g., 'Hann filter' | 'Ram-Lak filter' | 'Shepp-Logan filter' | 'Hamming filter' | 'Software default (not reported)'
column10: Sharper filters (Ram-Lak) enhance edge definition but amplify high-frequency noise; smoother filters (Hann, Hamming) reduce noise at the cost of edge sharpness.

column2: An externally-calibrated factor that converts the measured quantity into the reported quantity, how it was determined, and its uncertainty. Applies where the conversion depends on a factor calibrated against a reference of independently known value, rather than on the instrument response alone. Distinct from the fields that name the calibration material and that state which approach applies to which analyte, where the technique has them: this field records the resulting factor itself.

Physical constants and reference values used in data reduction to calculate the final reported quantity (e.g., decay constants for age calculation, standard isotope ratios, or other citable reference values used in a correction or calculation), together with their source. Distinct from the Group 6 reference-material fields, which document accepted values for specific calibration/validation materials rather than universal physical constants. Record "None" if no citable, revisable physical constants feed into this procedure's data reduction.

Effective spatial resolution of the reconstructed CT volume, which typically differs from (and is coarser than) the voxel size due to the detector point spread function (PSF), geometric unsharpness, and the reconstruction filter. Formal measurement uses the PSF method described in Ketcham & Hildebrandt (2014) or the modulation transfer function (MTF); resolution can also be reported per ASTM E1441-11. When formal measurement is unavailable, an estimate based on acquisition geometry (e.g., the Brenner-Weiss formula) or a stated multiple of the voxel size may be recorded. Report the value in µm along with the method used to determine or estimate it. Note that most XCT papers use the bare phrase "spatial resolution" for the voxel size; record that under Voxel Size, and leave this field as not reported unless an effective resolution was actually determined.

column2: Specification of how partial volume effects (PVE) are managed in quantitative analysis. PVE correction can be implemented via PSF-based deconvolution tools such as Blob3D. Record the minimum feature size criterion adopted for the procedure (in voxels or µm), the basis for it, the treatment of boundary voxels in modal abundance or size distribution calculations, and whether PVE correction is required or optional. State whether the criterion follows the Withers et al. (2021) convention — a feature must span at least 3 voxels to be positively identified and at least 10 for reliable shape and volume characterisation — or is SNR-limited, PVE-limited or analyst-defined.

column10: PVE produces intermediate CT numbers at phase boundaries and at the surfaces of small features, because each voxel integrates the attenuation of all material within its volume. The criterion materially changes reported modal abundances and size distributions, so two datasets are not comparable without it.

column2: Quantitative measure of image quality in the reconstructed CT volume.
